rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is a workable destination with a clear law-versus-practice gap. The legal framework is among the strongest in the region — it ranks 7th on a regional rights map, has banned conversion therapy and intersex infant surgery, has a hate-crime law covering gender identity, and legalised same-sex marriage in 2024. There are no trans-specific border or bathroom restrictions, and the government is progressive with an improving trajectory.

But the social reality lags the law. A mob of about 150 people assaulted two trans people in the second city; a regional human-rights court case documented police detention and mistreatment of trans sex workers; surveys show residents are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the regional average (63% avoid holding hands); and a foreign government's diplomatic guidance has issued an LGBTQ travel warning for this country. Major tourist destinations are welcoming; outside them the climate is rougher than the law suggests.

The consequence axis of an arrest is a documented default-plus-petition system: placement of trans women detainees started from the registered sex — the four trans women transferred to a women's prison facility on 4 December 2021 had previously been held in two other prisons, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender — and a decision of that date by the official responsible for crime-prevention policy created an on-request transfer route to women's facilities, the first documented transfers of trans prisoners to a women's facility in the country. No special trans units and no rule covering trans men's placement are documented. A detained trans visitor therefore meets a registered-sex default with an on-request transfer route that demonstrably exists but runs through administrative petition — a workable-but-request-dependent outcome consistent with the country's law-versus-practice gap.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Same-sex marriage legal since 2024 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners; the foreign government's LGBTQ travel warning is a general queer-traveler signal.

Custody-policy context: the 4 December 2021 transfer route was an administrative decision of the official responsible for crime-prevention policy (the transfers of the four women — three nationals of this country and one foreign national — followed each woman's petition), not legislation; an online overview of this country's LGBTQ rights confirms that placement starts from the registered sex, with the on-request transfer route for trans women — correctional-administration machinery, not a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
Resident-facing climate data from the sources: a 2024 regional survey of LGBTIQ residents records residents' avoidance and discrimination burden — 63% avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (regional average 53%), 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault, only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ, and 28% felt discriminated at work; the mob assault on two trans people in the second city and the documented police stops and mistreatment of transgender sex workers in the capital (the regional human-rights court case) fell on residents.

The documented custody practice is resident-facing: the registered-sex placement default and the 4 December 2021 on-request transfer route govern prisoners held in the national system — the documented transferees were a foreign national and three nationals of this country held in two prisons; a visitor meets the practice only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
No trans-specific travel advisory beyond the foreign government's general LGBTQ note; ordinary tourist-season crime affects all travellers.

Prison axis: how the on-request transfer route operates in practice — processing time, success rates, conditions before a transfer, and its application to a foreign visitor detained while travelling — is not documented; no trans special units and no rule covering trans men's placement appear in any source, the four December 2021 transfers are the only documented case series, and the online sources agree that default placement had followed the male facilities until that decision.
blindSourceSummaries: The legal framework: the country ranks 7th on a regional rights map, has banned conversion therapy and intersex infant surgery, has a hate-crime law covering gender identity, and legalised same-sex marriage in 2024; there are no trans-specific border or bathroom restrictions, and the government is progressive with an improving trajectory.

Social reality lagging the law: a mob of about 150 people assaulted two trans people in the second city; a regional human-rights court case documented police detention and mistreatment of trans sex workers; a 2024 regional survey records residents' avoidance and discrimination burden — 63% avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (regional average 53%), 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault, only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ, and 28% felt discriminated at work; a foreign government's diplomatic guidance has issued an LGBTQ travel warning for this country.

The custody practice: placement of trans women detainees started from the registered sex — the four trans women transferred to a women's prison facility on 4 December 2021 had previously been held in two other prisons, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender — and a decision of that date by the official responsible for crime-prevention policy created an on-request transfer route to women's facilities, the first documented transfers of trans prisoners to a women's facility in this country; the transferees were three nationals of this country and one foreign national; no special trans units and no rule covering trans men's placement are documented, and the sources agree that default placement had followed the male facilities until that decision.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under a national statute (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 of the country's state/province units apply religious law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender social-media personality was found beaten and dead on a highway in the capital; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the national statute has been described as a "weaponised" law — and gangs operating through dating apps lure victims into assault and robbery. A foreign government's diplomatic guidance has warned LGBT+ travellers to this country of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised nationally (the national statute targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the religious-law death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the foreign government's advisory make this an environment to avoid entirely.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented through the country's only recorded trans-imprisonment case: the country's most prominent transgender woman pleaded guilty to four counts of abuse of the national currency on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine, and served the term in a maximum-security prison, released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly questioned which prison the crossdresser would be kept in, and the article does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section — placement was discretionary — while an October 2024 investigative panel found the maximum-security placement itself unlawful for a first-time offender under the national correctional service act. For a trans visitor, the 14-year exposure under the national statute already applies to tourists; on top of that, detention would land in a prison system with a documented discretionary, unlawfully-assigned placement practice and no recorded housing standard for trans prisoners.
rewrites.blindTangential:
The national statute (14 years, applies to tourists) and the religious-law death penalty in 12 of the country's state/province units are direct risks for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; gangs operating through dating apps are a direct app-user risk.

Custody-litigation context: the only trans-prisoner "ruling" on record is the October 2024 investigative panel finding that the maximum-security placement in that case violated the national correctional service act because the prisoner was a first-time offender; the same panel dismissed the bribery allegations that had prompted it — an administrative outcome in a celebrity case, not a rule fixing trans-prisoner housing anywhere in the country.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The documented violence and impunity fall on residents: the killing of the trans social-media personality with no arrests six months on, police beatings and bribe-extortion of people perceived as gay, the attacks and lost job prospects documented a decade into the national statute's operation, and the law's documented reach beyond marriage — cohabitation, any public show of same-sex amorous relationship, and gay organisations criminalised with 10-14 years' prison, with police torture and arbitrary arrests under it (as documented in a 2016 human-rights report).

The recorded imprisonment case is a resident case: the person at its centre served her sentence in a national prison, and the discretionary placement practice (male or female section left unrecorded, the maximum-security assignment found unlawful for a first-time offender) governs residents held in the system — a visitor meets it only through arrest and detention, which the criminalisation of same-sex conduct makes a live prospect for trans visitors perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Terrorism, kidnapping, and violent crime affect all travellers in many regions; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Prison axis: no national law, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in any source in this record; the biography of the person in the recorded case does not record which section she was assigned to, the October 2024 panel finding concerns the lawfulness of a placement rather than a housing standard, and a news report on the proposed cross-dressing ban could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 401), so that bill's status rests on its written summary.
blindSourceSummaries: Criminalisation: same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under a national statute (14 years, applies to all including tourists), with 12 of the country's state/province units applying religious law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct; the statute's documented reach extends beyond marriage — cohabitation, any public show of same-sex amorous relationship, and gay organisations criminalised with 10-14 years' prison, with police torture and arbitrary arrests under it (documented in a 2016 human-rights report); police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" and the statute has been described as a "weaponised" law; a proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public, and trans identity is not explicitly criminalised nationally.

Violence and warnings: a transgender social-media personality was found beaten and dead on a highway in the capital, police misgendered her in death, and six months later no one had been arrested; gangs operating through dating apps lure victims into assault and robbery; a foreign government's diplomatic guidance has warned LGBT+ travellers to this country of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks; the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists.

The only recorded trans-imprisonment case: the country's most prominent transgender woman pleaded guilty to four counts of abuse of the national currency on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine, and served the term in a maximum-security prison, released on 5 August 2024; press coverage at sentencing openly questioned which prison the crossdresser would be kept in, and the article does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section — placement was discretionary; an October 2024 investigative panel found the maximum-security placement itself unlawful for a first-time offender under the national correctional service act; no national law, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing is documented in any source in this record.
